title: Arion · lines 1–6
subtitle: Arion makes his fortune in the Greek West and hires a Corinthian ship for the voyage home

units.en: Arion the cithara-singer, who spent most of his time at the court of Periander, tyrant of Corinth, was seized by a desire to sail to Italy and Sicily.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Arion is introduced by his profession straight away, so the reader sees him as a famous musician, which prepares for his final song on the ship.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.trans: the greater part of his time
notes.body: Herodotus stresses how long Arion stayed with Periander, which shows a close bond with a powerful patron who will matter later in the story.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Linking two destinations with τε καί highlights the distance and ambition of his tour, and so the risk of travelling so far by sea.

notes.label: Ring structure
notes.body: The journey starts at Corinth and is meant to end there, which frames the voyage neatly.

notes.label: Foreshadowing
notes.trans: having made a great deal of money
notes.body: The reader learns that Arion is carrying a fortune, and this becomes the crew's motive for trying to kill him.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Placing "great" at the end of the phrase draws attention to the size of his wealth.

notes.label: Parallelism
notes.body: Two matching verbs of wishing show that Arion's own desires drive the story and lead him into danger.

notes.label: Contrast (μέν … δέ)
notes.body: The balanced construction sets his departure against his trust in the Corinthians, which turns out to be his mistake.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: "Nobody" is a strong word that shows how complete his trust in the Corinthians was.

notes.label: Dramatic irony
notes.quote: πιστεύων δὲ οὐδαμοῖς μᾶλλον ἢ Κορινθίοις
notes.body: Arion trusts the Corinthians above everyone, yet they are the men who will betray him, so the reader feels uneasy on his behalf.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: Arion pays for the ship himself, which means he is hiring the very men who will try to murder him.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: The same word appears twice in different cases, which draws attention to the crew's nationality and reinforces the irony.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: Corinth is named four times, so the city dominates the passage and its people become central to the plot.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The crew's nationality comes at the very end of the sentence, so it is the last detail the reader is left with.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: A string of participles compresses years of travel into a few lines, which moves the story quickly towards the voyage and the real drama.

notes.label: Arion
notes.body: A poet and musician from Methymna on Lesbos, active around 600 BC. Herodotus says he was the finest cithara-singer of his day and the first to compose the dithyramb, a choral song for Dionysus, as a work of art.

notes.label: The cithara
notes.body: The cithara (κιθάρα) was the large concert version of the lyre, the instrument of professional performers. A κιθαρῳδός sang to his own accompaniment on it.

notes.label: Periander
notes.body: Ruler of Corinth from about 627 to 587 BC, under whom the city was rich and powerful. A τύραννος was a man who held sole power in a city without inheriting it as a king; the word did not necessarily mean that he was cruel.

notes.label: Corinth
notes.body: A wealthy trading city on the Isthmus, the strip of land joining the Peloponnese to central Greece, with harbours on both sides.

notes.label: The Greek West
notes.body: Southern Italy and Sicily were full of Greek cities, several of them Corinthian colonies (Syracuse was one). They were rich places where a famous performer could earn a fortune.

notes.label: Tarentum
notes.body: Taras (modern Taranto), a Spartan colony on the gulf in the instep of Italy, and a natural place to take ship for Greece.

questions: Herodotus mentions Arion's fortune before he says anything about the voyage. What does that lead you to expect?
Arion picks his ship because the crew are Corinthians. How does Herodotus make sure we notice that choice?

context.body:
Herodotus tells the story of Arion in Book 1 of the Histories (1.23–24), as an aside while he is describing Periander, ruler of Corinth. He says that the Corinthians and the people of Lesbos, Arion's home island, both tell it, and that in his day there was a small bronze figure at Taenarum of a man riding a dolphin, which Arion had dedicated there.

The tale was famous throughout antiquity. Dolphins were thought to love music, and they had a special connection with Apollo, patron of music and song: one story explained the name of his oracle at Delphi by saying that he had once appeared there in the form of a dolphin (δελφίς). A musician rescued by a dolphin is a musician the gods are looking after.

Watch how Herodotus tells it. The narrative is quick and plain, and most of the drama is carried by where he puts his words, by his participles, and by a handful of details that he chooses to repeat.
